title: IAAS
content:
1. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

    • Description: Provides virtualized computing resources over the internet, such as virtual machines, storage, and networking.

    • User Responsibility: Managing applications, data, runtime, and operating systems.

    • Provider Responsibility: Handling virtualization, servers, and physical infrastructure.

    • Example: AWS EC2, where users can launch and configure virtual servers.

    • Analogy: Like renting a plot of land—you build and manage everything on it.

  2. Platform as a Service (PaaS)

    • Description: Offers a platform for developing, running, and managing applications without the complexity of maintaining infrastructure.

    • User Responsibility: Managing applications and data.

    • Provider Responsibility: Managing runtime, middleware, operating systems, and infrastructure.

    • Example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which automates application deployment and scaling.

    • Analogy: Like renting an apartment—you furnish and decorate it, but the landlord handles maintenance.

  3. Software as a Service (SaaS)

    • Description: Delivers fully functional software applications over the internet, accessible via a web browser.

    • User Responsibility: Simply using the software.

    • Provider Responsibility: Managing everything, including the application and infrastructure.

    • Example: Google Workspace (e.g., Gmail, Google Docs).

    • Analogy: Like staying in a hotel—everything is provided, and you just use the services.

This error means your deployment/build system no longer supports Node.js 18.x, and you need to upgrade to Node.js 22.x.

Here’s how you can fix it depending on your setup:

If using Vercel

  1. Go to your project dashboard on Vercel.

  2. Navigate to Project Settings → General → Node.js Version.

  3. Select 22.x from the dropdown.

  4. Redeploy your project.

title: S3 notes
content:
Features of Amazon S3

Storage classes

Amazon S3 offers a range of storage classes designed for different use cases. For example, you can store mission-critical production data in S3 Standard or S3 Express One Zone for frequent access, save costs by storing infrequently accessed data in S3 Standard-IA or S3 One Zone-IA, and archive data at the lowest costs in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-zone Amazon S3 storage class that is purpose-built to deliver consistent, single-digit millisecond data access for your most latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone is the lowest latency cloud object storage class available today, with data access speeds up to 10x faster and with request costs 50 percent lower than S3 Standard. S3 Express One Zone is the first S3 storage class where you can select a single Availability Zone with the option to co-locate your object storage with your compute resources, which provides the highest possible access speed. Additionally, to further increase access speed and support hundreds of thousands of requests per second, data is stored in a new bucket type: an Amazon S3 directory bucket. For more information, see S3 Express One Zone and Working with directory buckets.

You can store data with changing or unknown access patterns in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which optimizes storage costs by automatically moving your data between four access tiers when your access patterns change. These four access tiers include two low-latency access tiers optimized for frequent and infrequent access, and two opt-in archive access tiers designed for asynchronous access for rarely accessed data.

For more information, see Understanding and managing Amazon S3 storage classes.

Storage management

Amazon S3 has storage management features that you can use to manage costs, meet regulatory requirements, reduce latency, and save multiple distinct copies of your data for compliance requirements.

  • S3 Lifecycle – Configure a lifecycle configuration to manage your objects and store them cost effectively throughout their lifecycle. You can transition objects to other S3 storage classes or expire objects that reach the end of their lifetimes.

  • S3 Object Lock – Prevent Amazon S3 objects from being deleted or overwritten for a fixed amount of time or indefinitely. You can use Object Lock to help meet regulatory requirements that require write-once-read-many (WORM) storage or to simply add another layer of protection against object changes and deletions.

  • S3 Replication – Replicate objects and their respective metadata and object tags to one or more destination buckets in the same or different AWS Regions for reduced latency, compliance, security, and other use cases.

  • S3 Batch Operations – Manage billions of objects at scale with a single S3 API request or a few clicks in the Amazon S3 console. You can use Batch Operations to perform operations such as Copy, Invoke AWS Lambda function, and Restore on millions or billions of objects.

content: <p>Patterns for building apps with LLMs: You send data to LLM endpoints so ChatGPT, Claude and we receive a prediction back which is our result. (Input, transformation and output) - This process is called inference. The data is typically formatted as messages, such as prompts, queries, knowledge bases, specifications which serve as memory. Inference: Is the computational process that happens inside the LLM when it generates the prediction or output from the input. Broader Inference Pipeline: User Input → API Request → [INFERENCE happens here] → API Response → User Output Inference is the middle where the model does its computation. When you call OpenAI's API or Anthropic's API, you're not directly doing inference - you're requesting that their servers perform inference for you. The inference happens on their GPUs/TPUs, not in your API call. Context Engineering AI Engineering is basically context engineering, its the heart of AI Engineering. As an AI Engineer you become a context architect, designing what infromation a model sees, when it sees it and how its structured to get the best outputs. We give the models the right information to give us a response or prediction. Handling data types at scale, there is an emerging LLM App Stack, applications are becoming the orchestration layers. What Context Engineering Really Involves Think of it as information architecture for LLMs: Raw Data → Context Design → Formatted Prompt → LLM → Useful Output Key Components: Prompt Engineering: Crafting instructions and examples RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): Pulling relevant documents/data into context Context Window Management: Fitting the right information within token limits Dynamic Context Construction: Building prompts programmatically based on user state, retrieved data, and task requirements Orchestration Layers: Modern applications are becoming orchestration systems which: Decide what context to retrieve Which tools and functions LLMs should access Route between different models based on the tasks Manage convos and state Chain multiple LLM calls together with logic The Emerging LLM stack: Application Layer (your code) ↓ Orchestration (LangChain, LlamaIndex, custom logic) ↓ Context Sources (Vector DBs, APIs, Documents) ↓ LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) ↓ Infrastructure (Caching, Monitoring, Guards) Why Context Engineering > Prompt Engineering While prompt engineering focuses on crafting the perfect instruction, context engineering is about: Data Pipeline Design: How do you get from messy real-world data to clean, relevant context? Retrieval Strategy: What information do you surface and when? Context Prioritization: With limited tokens, what's most important? State Management: How do you maintain coherence across multiple interactions? AWS / Cloud Platforms sit on every single layer of this stack. From the application layer, to orchestration, to context to LLMs to infrastructure. Tools like bedrock make it easy as they are a single unified platform to run and manage LLMs.</p>

Microsoft Spark refers to the integration of Apache Spark within Microsoft's data analytics and cloud platforms, particularly Azure Synapse Analytics and Microsoft Fabric. It provides a powerful engine for data processing, machine learning, and big data analytics, leveraging Spark's in-memory computing capabilities for speed and efficiency. Microsoft also offers tools like Microsoft Spark Utilities (MSSparkUtils) to simplify common tasks within Spark environments. 

Here's a more detailed breakdown:

1. Apache Spark and Microsoft's Implementations:

  • Apache Spark:

    A distributed computing framework designed for fast, in-memory processing of large datasets. 

  • Azure Synapse Analytics:

    Microsoft's platform for big data analytics and enterprise data warehousing, offering serverless Apache Spark pools for processing data stored in Azure. 

  • Microsoft Fabric:

    A comprehensive, all-in-one analytics solution that includes a fully managed Apache Spark compute platform for data engineering and data science workloads. 

2. Key Features and Benefits:

  • Speed and Efficiency:

    Spark's in-memory processing allows for faster execution of data analysis and machine learning tasks compared to disk-based systems. 

  • Scalability and Flexibility:

    Spark can handle large volumes of data and is compatible with various data sources, including Azure Storage and Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. 

  • Programming Language Support:

    Spark integrates with multiple programming languages (Python, Scala, .NET, and R) enabling diverse data manipulation capabilities. 

  • Microsoft Spark Utilities (MSSparkUtils):

    A built-in package in Synapse and Fabric that simplifies common tasks like file system operations, environment variable management, notebook chaining, and secret handling. 

  • Optimized Performance:

    Microsoft Fabric provides starter pools for rapid Spark session initialization and offers customization options for tailored analytics experiences. 

3. Use Cases:

  • Data Engineering:

    Processing and transforming large datasets for data warehousing and other analytical purposes. 

  • Data Science:

    Building and deploying machine learning models using Spark's machine learning libraries. 

  • Real-time Analytics:

    Enabling fast data processing and analysis for interactive applications. 

  • Notebook-based Workflows:

    Using Spark within notebooks for interactive exploration and analysis of data. 

4. Integration with Other Microsoft Services:

  • Azure Storage and Data Lake Storage Gen2: Spark pools in Synapse are compatible with these storage solutions. 

  • Microsoft Fabric: Fabric's data engineering and data science experiences are built on a Spark compute platform. 

  • Microsoft Entra: Used for authentication and authorization in Synapse and Fabric environments.

Machine Learning: The Engine Powering the AI Revolution

1. Introduction

Machine Learning (ML) is no longer a niche area of computer science — it’s the beating heart of modern artificial intelligence. From Netflix recommending your next binge-worthy show to self-driving cars navigating city streets, ML is silently reshaping industries and our daily lives.

But what exactly is it? At its core, machine learning is the science of teaching computers to learn patterns from data and make decisions or predictions without being explicitly programmed.

2. How Machine Learning Works

The process of machine learning can be simplified into three main steps:

  1. Data Collection – Gathering relevant data (images, text, numbers, sensor readings, etc.).

  2. Training – Feeding data into algorithms that learn from examples.

  3. Prediction/Inference – Using the trained model to make predictions on new, unseen data.

The better the quality of the data, the more accurate the model will be — a concept often summed up as “garbage in, garbage out.”

3. Types of Machine Learning

A. Supervised Learning

  • The model learns from labeled examples (input + correct output).

  • Used for: Email spam detection, stock price prediction, medical diagnosis.

  • Common algorithms: Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Support Vector Machines, Neural Networks

title: ECS
content:
Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) is a fully managed container orchestration service that allows you to deploy, manage, and scale Docker containers on Amazon Web Services (AWS). It simplifies the process by handling the underlying infrastructure, so you can focus on your applications rather than managing servers or the control plane. ECS integrates deeply with other AWS services like Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and offers two main compute options: running containers on your own managed Amazon EC2 instances or using the serverless AWS Fargate option. 

Key Features and Capabilities

  • Fully Managed:

    Amazon ECS manages the underlying infrastructure, eliminating the need to provision or scale servers for your containers. 

  • Container Orchestration:

    It orchestrates your containers, scheduling their placement based on resource needs and availability requirements. 

  • Seamless Integration:

    ECS integrates natively with other core AWS services, including security groups, Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes, and IAM, for enhanced security and functionality. 

  • Launch Types:

    You can choose to run your containers on serverless AWS Fargate or on Amazon EC2 instances that you manage. 

  • Application Scaling:

    You can easily scale your containerized applications up or down by adjusting the desired number of tasks. 

  • Monitoring and Logging:

    With built-in integrations with Amazon CloudWatch, you can collect and monitor metrics and logs from your containers. 

  • Service Connect:

    This feature simplifies service discovery and connectivity for your containerized microservices.

🚋 The Tram: The City’s Silent Connector

Trams, often called streetcars or trolleys, are one of the most efficient and sustainable modes of urban transportation. Running on rails embedded in city streets, they bridge the gap between buses and trains — offering the convenience of road transport with the smooth efficiency of rail travel.

Originating in the 19th century, early trams were pulled by horses before evolving into electric-powered systems, revolutionizing public transit across Europe, Asia, and North America. Today, modern trams are celebrated for their eco-friendliness, energy efficiency, and ability to reduce traffic congestion in busy urban centers.

Beyond functionality, trams have become a symbol of smart cities — blending nostalgia with innovation. Cities like Amsterdam, Melbourne, Zurich, and Hiroshima have integrated tram networks as vital arteries of their public transport systems, ensuring accessibility for millions daily.

Modern trams now feature low-floor designs for accessibility, digital route displays, quiet electric motors, and even AI-assisted traffic coordination to optimize routes and energy use.

In a world striving toward greener mobility, trams represent more than just transport — they embody a commitment to sustainability, community connectivity, and urban livability

An "RLS policy" refers to a Row-Level Security policy, a database security feature that controls access to specific rows within a table, rather than entire tables. These policies allow administrators to define rules based on user group membership or execution context, ensuring that users only see or modify data relevant to their role, such as a worker only seeing data for their department. The access logic is built directly into the database, creating a more reliable and robust security layer for applications.
 

How RLS Policies Work

  • Implicit WHERE Clauses:

    RLS policies essentially add a WHERE clause to every query a user attempts on a specific table. 

  • Enforcement at the Database Tier:

    The security logic is enforced by the database itself, not in client or application code, which simplifies security management and reduces potential vulnerabilities. 

  • Fine-Grained Control:

    Policies can define restrictions for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements, providing comprehensive control over data access and modifications.

title: Cloud Comp
content:
Definition of Cloud Computing

Cloud computing is a model for delivering computing resources. Such as servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and analytics, over the internet.

Rather than owning and maintaining physical hardware or software, users access these resources on-demand from a cloud provider’s data centers. This approach offers flexibility, scalability, and cost-efficiency, as users pay only for what they use.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines cloud computing as::

"A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g., networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction."

In simpler terms, cloud computing is like renting computing power and storage from a provider, similar to renting an apartment or car, but for technology resources.

Evolution of Cloud Computing

Cloud computing has evolved significantly over the decades, driven by technological advancements and business needs:

  • 1960s-1970s: The concept of time-sharing emerged, allowing multiple users to access a single mainframe computer simultaneously. This idea of shared resources laid the groundwork for cloud computing.

  • 1990s: The internet’s growth and the development of virtualization technologies enabled virtual machines (VMs), allowing multiple operating systems to run on a single physical server.

  • Early 2000s: Companies like Salesforce pioneered Software as a Service (SaaS), delivering applications over the internet without requiring local installation.

  • 2006: Amazon Web Services (AWS) launched, introducing Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) with services like Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) and Simple Storage Service (S3). This marked the beginning of modern cloud computing.

  • 2010s-Present: Cloud adoption surged, with the introduction of Platform as a Service (PaaS), hybrid clouds, and advanced offerings like artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in the cloud.

Today, cloud computing powers businesses globally, enabling innovation, scalability, and accessibility.

Cloud Service Models

Cloud computing is categorized into three primary service models, each offering different levels of control, flexibility, and management responsibility:

title: Untitled
content:
1. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

    • Description: Provides virtualized computing resources over the internet, such as virtual machines, storage, and networking.

    • User Responsibility: Managing applications, data, runtime, and operating systems.

    • Provider Responsibility: Handling virtualization, servers, and physical infrastructure.

    • Example: AWS EC2, where users can launch and configure virtual servers.

    • Analogy: Like renting a plot of land—you build and manage everything on it.

  2. Platform as a Service (PaaS)

    • Description: Offers a platform for developing, running, and managing applications without the complexity of maintaining infrastructure.

    • User Responsibility: Managing applications and data.

    • Provider Responsibility: Managing runtime, middleware, operating systems, and infrastructure.

    • Example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which automates application deployment and scaling.

    • Analogy: Like renting an apartment—you furnish and decorate it, but the landlord handles maintenance.

  3. Software as a Service (SaaS)

    • Description: Delivers fully functional software applications over the internet, accessible via a web browser.

    • User Responsibility: Simply using the software.

    • Provider Responsibility: Managing everything, including the application and infrastructure.

    • Example: Google Workspace (e.g., Gmail, Google Docs).

    • Analogy: Like staying in a hotel—everything is provided, and you just use the services.

title: S3 Vectors
content:
S3 Vectors

Amazon S3 Vectors provides cost-effective, elastic, and durable vector storage at up to 90% lower costs for uploading, storing, and querying vectors. With S3 Vectors, you can power RAG and other semantic search workloads at scale, at a fraction of the cost for storage, requests, data uploaded, and data queried.

PUT cost
PUT pricing is based on logical GB of the vectors you upload, where each vector is the sum of its logical vector data, metadata, and key. You can upload multiple vectors in a single PUT request, maximizing upload throughput and minimizing upload costs.

Storage cost
Total storage is the sum of logical storage across your indexes, where the size of your storage is determined by the number of vectors you store and their size.  Vector size is determined by:

1) Vector data: Each vector has a size determined by number of dimensions. Each dimension equals 4 bytes of storage per vector, so for example, a 1024-dimensional vector requires 4 KB of logical vector data.

2) Metadata: You can store both filterable and non-filterable metadata with your vector. Non-filterable metadata is used to return information as a part of query results while filterable metadata can also be used to filter query results.

3) Key: Each vector is associated with a key. Keys require 1 byte of storage per character.

Query cost
Query charges include a per API charge in addition to a $/TB charge based on the average vector size, including vector data, key, and filterable metadata, multiplied by the number of vectors in the index you’re querying. As your vector index grows, data processing charges for query increase proportionally; however, at larger scale, you benefit from lower $/TB pricing above 100K  in your vector index.
